families.label: Instrumental variables
families.definition: An instrument that shifts the treatment but affects the outcome only through it identifies the effect for those whose treatment the instrument moves.

families.label: Difference in differences
families.definition: The change in the outcome of a treated group is compared with the change of an untreated group over the same period; parallel trends do the identifying work.

families.label: Event study
families.definition: Outcomes are traced before and after an event at the individual level, so pre-event trends are visible and the effect is read from the post-event deviation.

families.label: Regression discontinuity
families.definition: A rule assigns treatment at a threshold of a running variable; units just above and just below the cutoff are compared.

families.label: Fixed effects (within variation)
families.definition: Time-invariant differences between units are removed by comparing each unit with itself over time or across its own members.

families.label: Sibling and family comparison
families.definition: Siblings or other family members are compared with one another, holding everything shared within the family fixed.

families.label: Twin comparison
families.definition: Twins are compared with one another, holding shared genes and upbringing fixed.

families.label: Matching
families.definition: Each treated unit is paired with untreated units that look alike on observables, and their outcomes are compared.

families.label: Selection on observables
families.definition: Treated and untreated units are compared after adjusting for observed characteristics, assuming nothing unobserved drives both treatment and outcome.

families.label: Randomised controlled trial
families.definition: Treatment is assigned at random by the researchers or a programme, so the treated and the untreated are alike in expectation.

families.label: Lottery
families.definition: Treatment is allocated by an actual lottery outside the researchers' control, such as an admission or housing lottery.

families.label: Bunching
families.definition: The mass of units piling up at a kink or notch of an incentive schedule reveals the behavioural response to the incentive.

families.label: Synthetic control
families.definition: A weighted combination of untreated units is built to track the treated unit before treatment; the gap afterwards is the effect.

families.label: Structural model
families.definition: An economic model is estimated and its parameters, not a reduced-form contrast, carry the causal content.

families.label: Other designs
families.definition: Designs that fit none of the families above.

families.label: Descriptive
families.definition: No identification strategy is claimed; the estimate describes an association or a gap.

sub_designs.label: Continuous exposure (dose-response)
sub_designs.definition: Units differ in the intensity of exposure to the change rather than in a treated/untreated split.

sub_designs.label: Staggered adoption
sub_designs.definition: Units are treated at different dates; later-treated units serve as controls for earlier ones.

sub_designs.label: Two-period policy change
sub_designs.definition: One reform at one date; treated and untreated groups before and after.

sub_designs.label: firm-level shock to fixed cohort
sub_designs.definition: Workers are grouped into cohorts by their pre-shock employer and tracked after that employer receives a shock, so cohort composition is fixed before the shock.

sub_designs.label: Individual shock
sub_designs.definition: The event is a shock to the individual: job loss, illness, death of a relative, divorce.

sub_designs.label: Policy change
sub_designs.definition: The event is a reform or rule change at a known date.

sub_designs.label: job-spell fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Worker-firm job-spell fixed effects absorb all time-invariant characteristics of the match, so only within-spell changes in the firm's exposure identify the effect.

sub_designs.label: Two-way fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Unit and time fixed effects together.

sub_designs.label: Shift-share (Bartik) instrument
sub_designs.definition: Exposure of units to aggregate shifts, weighted by their initial shares, instruments the local change in the treatment.

sub_designs.label: Simulated (mechanical) policy instrument
sub_designs.definition: A mechanically simulated change in the treatment variable, computed by applying new policy rules to baseline (pre-period) behavior, instruments the actual change in treatment.

sub_designs.label: matched comparison group
sub_designs.definition: Treated units are paired with untreated units on observed characteristics to form a comparison group, without a specified propensity-score or exact-cell rule.

sub_designs.label: predicted-effect accounting
sub_designs.definition: Previously estimated elasticities are applied to observed changes in exposure to compute predicted outcome changes across the distribution, without new identification.

sub_designs.label: Age or date cutoff
sub_designs.definition: The running variable is age or a calendar date.

sub_designs.label: Fuzzy cutoff
sub_designs.definition: The probability of treatment jumps at the threshold; the jump instruments treatment.

sub_designs.label: Regression adjustment
sub_designs.definition: Covariates enter a regression; the treatment coefficient is the estimate.

sub_designs.label: Synthetic control
sub_designs.definition: A donor pool weighted to match the treated unit before treatment.

sub_designs.label: Judge or caseworker leniency
sub_designs.definition: The leniency of the randomly assigned decision-maker instruments the decision taken for the individual.

sub_designs.label: Lottery or random assignment as instrument
sub_designs.definition: A lottery or random assignment instruments actual take-up of the treatment.

sub_designs.label: Distance or access
sub_designs.definition: Distance to, or local availability of, a service or institution instruments its use.

sub_designs.label: Policy eligibility rule
sub_designs.definition: A rule that makes some units eligible for a programme instruments participation.

sub_designs.label: Timing of birth or cohort
sub_designs.definition: The month or year of birth relative to a rule instruments the treatment, such as school starting age.

sub_designs.label: Peer or network exposure
sub_designs.definition: Exposure of peers or network members to a shock instruments the individual's treatment.

sub_designs.label: Weather or natural shock
sub_designs.definition: A natural event such as rainfall, temperature or a disaster instruments the treatment.

sub_designs.label: Health or mortality shock
sub_designs.definition: An illness or death, treated as unforeseeable, instruments a change in circumstances.

sub_designs.label: Other instrument
sub_designs.definition: An instrument of another kind.

sub_designs.label: Triple difference
sub_designs.definition: A second untreated dimension removes group-specific shocks from the difference in differences.

sub_designs.label: Family event
sub_designs.definition: The event is a birth, a marriage or another change in the family.

sub_designs.label: Sharp cutoff
sub_designs.definition: Treatment switches deterministically at the threshold.

sub_designs.label: Regression kink
sub_designs.definition: The slope, not the level, of the treatment changes at the threshold.

sub_designs.label: Geographic boundary
sub_designs.definition: The running variable is distance to a border between regimes.

sub_designs.label: Individual fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Each person is compared with themself over time.

sub_designs.label: Firm or establishment fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Each firm or workplace is compared with itself over time.

sub_designs.label: Mover design
sub_designs.definition: Units that move between places, firms or regimes identify place or firm effects.

sub_designs.label: Sibling fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Siblings compared within the family.

sub_designs.label: Extended family comparison
sub_designs.definition: Cousins or other relatives compared within the extended family.

sub_designs.label: Twin fixed effects
sub_designs.definition: Twins compared within the pair.

sub_designs.label: Propensity score matching
sub_designs.definition: Matching on the estimated probability of treatment.

sub_designs.label: Exact or coarsened matching
sub_designs.definition: Matching on the values, or coarsened values, of chosen covariates.

sub_designs.label: Nearest-neighbour matching
sub_designs.definition: Matching on a distance over covariates.

sub_designs.label: Reweighting
sub_designs.definition: Untreated units are reweighted to resemble the treated on observables.

sub_designs.label: Field experiment
sub_designs.definition: Randomisation by the researchers in the field.

sub_designs.label: Randomised policy pilot
sub_designs.definition: A programme randomised by the implementing agency.

sub_designs.label: Survey or laboratory experiment
sub_designs.definition: Randomisation inside a survey or laboratory setting.

sub_designs.label: Admission lottery
sub_designs.definition: Oversubscribed school or programme places allocated by lottery.

sub_designs.label: Allocation lottery
sub_designs.definition: Housing, land or other goods allocated by lottery.

sub_designs.label: Bunching at a kink
sub_designs.definition: Excess mass at a kink of the schedule.

sub_designs.label: Bunching at a notch
sub_designs.definition: Excess mass and a hole around a notch of the schedule.

sub_designs.label: Dynamic discrete choice
sub_designs.definition: A dynamic programming model of choices estimated on the data.

sub_designs.label: Search or matching model
sub_designs.definition: A labour market search or matching model.

sub_designs.label: Life-cycle model
sub_designs.definition: A model of consumption, saving, labour supply or schooling over the life cycle.

sub_designs.label: Sufficient statistics
sub_designs.definition: A formula from theory combines estimated elasticities into a welfare or policy effect.

sub_designs.label: Other structural model
sub_designs.definition: A structural model of another kind.

sub_designs.label: Other
sub_designs.definition: A design of another kind.

patterns.label: Differences in X across units, conditional on observed covariates, identify X's effect on Y
patterns.definition: Treatment varies across units in the cross-section and identification rests on controlling for observed characteristics, with no unit fixed effects to absorb unobserved heterogeneity.

patterns.label: Units experience differently sized changes in X over time; Y is compared across units and periods
patterns.definition: Identification comes from differential, continuously measured changes in the treatment across units over time, with outcomes compared across units and periods.

patterns.label: A policy reaches units at different dates; Y is compared around each unit's date
Variation in X within units over time, net of unit and unit-by-period fixed effects, identifies X's effect on Y
patterns.definition: Unit and period (or unit-by-period) fixed effects absorb level differences and common shocks so that only within-unit, over-time variation in the treatment identifies the outcome response.

patterns.label: A policy change raises X in one unit; Y is compared with a weighted combination of untreated units
patterns.definition: The treated unit's post-policy outcome is compared with a weighted average of untreated units chosen to match its pre-policy path, attributing the divergence to the policy-induced change in treatment.

patterns.label: A rule assigns X at a threshold of a running variable; Y is compared across the cutoff
The timing of a shock to the individual (job loss, illness, death) identifies its effect on Y
A policy grants X only to units above an eligibility threshold; Y is compared between just-above and just-below units be
patterns.definition: Eligibility for a policy is determined by an administrative threshold, and outcomes for units above the threshold are compared with those just below it before and after the policy takes effect.

patterns.label: a mechanical change in X predicted by applying changed policy rules to baseline behavior instruments X's effect on Y
patterns.definition: Policy rules are applied to units' base-period characteristics to compute the change in X they would mechanically experience, and this simulated change instruments the observed change in X in estimating its effect on Y.

patterns.label: A shift in exposure to X across units instruments X's effect on Y
pattern.exposure_of_pre_shock_cohort_to_predicted_change
patterns.definition: A cohort fixed before a shock is exposed to an externally predicted change in X, and its subsequent change in Y is compared across differently exposed cohorts.

patterns.label: pattern.estimated_elasticities_applied_to_observed_changes_in_x
patterns.definition: Estimated elasticities of Y with respect to X are applied to observed changes in X to compute predicted changes in Y across units.

units.summary: A multinomial logit of players' country choice includes country and country-by-year fixed effects plus a home dummy, so only residual variation in the net-of-tax rate each player faces (including eligibility and duration rules of preferential schemes for foreigners) identifies the location elasticity.
units.source_of_variation: All sources of variation in top earnings tax rates across the 14 sample countries and over time in the post-Bosman era, including preferential tax schemes for immigrants (columns 3-6 use variation within country and year in the net-of-tax rates facing different players, e.g. the eligibility and duration rules of the preferential schemes)

units.summary: Countries changed their top net-of-tax rates by different amounts over the post-Bosman period, and comparing how the location of domestic and foreign players moved across these differentially treated countries over time identifies the tax elasticity of migration.
units.source_of_variation: All sources of variation in top earnings tax rates across the 14 sample countries and over time in the post-Bosman era, including preferential tax schemes for immigrants (column 2 uses differential variation over time across countries, a difference-in-differences strategy)

units.summary: Spain's 2004 'Beckham law' cut the tax rate on arriving foreigners, and the post-reform jump in the share of foreign players relative to a synthetic control country (and relative to foreigners ineligible under the ten-year residence rule) identifies the migration elasticity.
units.instrument: 1(c = T) x 1(t >= t0): treatment-country dummy interacted with the post-reform dummy
units.source_of_variation: The 2004 Spanish 'Beckham law' (Royal Decree 687/2005), a flat 24 percent tax in lieu of the regular progressive income tax for foreign workers moving to Spain on or after 1 January 2004, compared with a synthetic control country and, within Spain, between foreigners eligible and ineligible under the ten-year residence rule

units.summary: Denmark's 1992 flat-tax scheme for high-income foreigners sharply raised their net-of-tax rate, and the divergence of Denmark's share of foreign players from a synthetic control country after the reform identifies the elasticity of foreign supply.
units.instrument: 1(c = T) x 1(t >= t0): treatment-country dummy interacted with the post-reform dummy
units.source_of_variation: The Danish preferential flat-tax scheme enacted in 1992 for foreign researchers and high-income foreigners signing employment contracts in Denmark after 1 June 1991 (a flat 25 percent, 30 percent in 1991-1995, in lieu of a regular top rate above 60 percent), compared with a synthetic control country

units.summary: Without country fixed effects, the specification uses raw cross-country differences in top net-of-tax rates, conditioning only on a home dummy and player characteristics, to relate tax levels to where players choose to play.
units.source_of_variation: All sources of variation in top earnings tax rates across the 14 sample countries and over time in the post-Bosman era, including preferential tax schemes for immigrants (column 1 uses the cross-country variation with no country fixed effects)

units.summary: The Danish scheme's earnings-eligibility rule splits arriving foreigners into an eligible group and a just-below-threshold control group, and the post-1991 divergence in their numbers (reinforced after the 1996 Bosman deregulation) measures the scheme's pull on high-earning foreign workers.
units.source_of_variation: The 1992 Danish preferential flat-tax scheme for highly paid foreign workers arriving in Denmark in 1991 or after, whose earnings-threshold eligibility rule splits foreigners into a treatment and a just-below-threshold control group, interacted with the 1996 Bosman deregulation of the football labor market

units.summary: Being born just after the January 1 enrollment cutoff raises school starting age discontinuously but imperfectly, so the cutoff indicator instruments actual starting age in a fuzzy RD on children's SDQ symptom scores.
units.instrument: 1(day_i >= 0), an indicator for being born on January 1 or later, instrumenting school starting age
units.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

atlas.from_label: Parents' age at the child's birth

units.summary: Comparing children born just before and just after the January 1 enrollment cutoff gives the reduced-form jump in school starting age and in SDQ difficulties, since birth timing around the date is as good as random.
units.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

units.summary: An OLS regression of SDQ inattention/hyperactivity on observed school starting age with covariates is reported as a descriptive benchmark that the authors argue is contaminated by parental selection.
units.source_of_variation: none: ordinary least squares on observed school starting age, used to motivate the RD design

units.summary: Individuals who received an unanticipated inheritance after the sudden death of their last surviving parent are compared with matched non-recipients (and windfall-induced entrepreneurs with other entrepreneurs) on income, wealth and business survival, so the death-driven liquidity shock rather than selection drives the contrast.
units.source_of_variation: Windfall wealth from unexpected inheritance due to the sudden death of the last living parent (or of both parents within the same calendar year) in Denmark, 1995-2001; 12,068 sudden household terminations with 19,329 beneficiaries identified from ICD-10 causes of death

units.summary: Because the size of the windfall varies across beneficiaries of an unanticipated parental death, before-after changes in entrepreneurial entry and performance are compared across heirs receiving larger versus smaller inheritances.
units.source_of_variation: Windfall wealth from unexpected inheritance due to the sudden death of the last living parent (or of both parents within the same calendar year) in Denmark, 1995-2001; 12,068 sudden household terminations with 19,329 beneficiaries identified from ICD-10 causes of death

units.summary: Within the sample of windfall heirs who started firms, entrepreneurial profit is regressed on observed ability proxies (age, schooling, pre-entrepreneurship income), attributing differences in performance to these characteristics conditional on covariates.
units.source_of_variation: Windfall wealth from unexpected inheritance due to the sudden death of the last living parent (or of both parents within the same calendar year) in Denmark, 1995-2001; 12,068 sudden household terminations with 19,329 beneficiaries identified from ICD-10 causes of death

units.summary: Couples who emigrated are compared with observationally similar couples who stayed in Denmark, matched on partners' education, children, age and period, so that any later difference in the wife's labor force participation is attributed to migration under the assumption of no selection on unobservables.
units.source_of_variation: Comparison of migrant couples (emigrating in 2001 or 2002) with nonmigrant couples observed in Denmark in 2001 and 2008, matched on observable characteristics; the authors state they have no natural experiment

units.outcome: growth in labor and capital income
units.summary: Successive Danish tax reforms mechanically changed marginal net-of-tax rates differently across income levels, income compositions and income types, so the simulated three-year change in the net-of-tax rate under base-year behavior instruments the actual change and identifies taxable income elasticities.
units.instrument: Three-year growth rate in the simulated marginal net-of-tax rate under base-year behavior (mechanical tax variation from tax reforms); virtual income is instrumented analogously where included.
units.source_of_variation: Mechanical (simulated) changes in marginal net-of-tax rates generated by the series of Danish tax reforms between 1984 and 2005, including the large 1987 reform and the 1994 reform; identification comes from tax changes that differ across income levels, across taxpayers at the same income level with different income composition, and across income types.

units.summary: The 1987 reform raised the marginal net-of-tax rate for some taxpayer groups and lowered it for others, so comparing income before (1986) and after (1989) between these groups identifies the income response, with the group-by-post interaction instrumenting the log net-of-tax rate.
units.instrument: Interaction between the after-reform time dummy and the treatment-group dummy, instrumenting the log marginal net-of-tax rate
units.source_of_variation: The Danish 1987 tax reform (passed in parliament during 1986, tax rates changed starting 1987), which raised the marginal net-of-tax rate for some groups of taxpayers and lowered it for others; treatment and control groups are defined by the reform-induced 1986–1989 change in the marginal net-of-tax rate shown in Figure 3.

units.summary: Workers' training take-up is traced around the date of a firm mass layoff (at least 30 percent of the workforce gone), with displaced and staying workers split by whether their firm's predicted offshoring — driven by foreign supply shocks — rose, so the layoff timing supplies the shock and the offshoring split the exposure.
units.source_of_variation: Firm-level mass-layoff events (1998–2006) combined with firm-level increases in predicted offshoring between t−1 and t, where predicted offshoring is taken from HJMX 2011 and is driven by foreign supply shocks.

units.summary: Country-product-year shocks external to Denmark (world export supply, world import demand, transport costs), aggregated to each firm with its pre-sample 1994 trade shares, instrument within-job-spell changes in firm offshoring and exports in wage regressions.
units.instrument: Firm-level weighted averages of log world export supply, log world import demand and log transport costs (for imports and for exports), weights = firm's pre-sample (1994) country-product import/export
units.source_of_variation: Within-job-spell, over-time variation in the employing firm's imports and exports driven by country x product x year shocks external to Denmark: world export supply (WES), world import demand (WID) and estimated transport costs, aggregated to the firm with pre-sample (1994) country-product trade shares.

units.summary: Worker cohorts defined by employment at a firm in a pre-shock base year are followed forward, and their subsequent change in average wages is regressed on the change in the firm's offshoring predicted by external world trade shocks, so composition and selection are fixed before the shock.
units.instrument: Firm-level weighted averages of log world export supply, log world import demand and log transport costs (for imports and for exports), weights = firm's pre-sample (1994) country-product import/export
units.source_of_variation: The change in PREDICTED firm-level offshoring between the base year and the following year, built from the first-stage IV regressions of Section IV (world export supply, world import demand and transport costs weighted by pre-sample country-product trade shares), for cohorts fixed before the shock

units.summary: Wages are regressed on the employing firm's observed offshoring and exports using only within-job-spell variation plus industry-year and regional fixed effects, assuming these changes are unrelated to the wage residual.
units.source_of_variation: Within-job-spell, over-time variation in the employing firm's narrow offshoring and exports, with no instrumenting

units.summary: First-stage within-job-spell regressions show that firm-level offshoring and exports respond to world export supply, world import demand and transport-cost shocks aggregated with pre-sample country-product trade shares.
units.source_of_variation: Within-job-spell, over-time variation in the employing firm's imports and exports driven by country x product x year shocks external to Denmark: world export supply (WES), world import demand (WID) and estimated transport costs, aggregated to the firm with pre-sample (1994) country-product trade shares.

units.summary: Observed year-on-year changes in firms' offshoring and exports are combined with the instrumented wage elasticities to compute predicted wage changes bin by bin, inheriting the identification of the earlier FE-IV estimates.
units.instrument: Firm-level weighted averages of log world export supply, log world import demand and log transport costs (for imports and for exports), weights = firm's pre-sample (1994) country-product import/export
units.source_of_variation: Observed year-on-year variation in firms' offshoring and exports, combined with the instrumented wage elasticities of Table 5

units.summary: Medical subdistricts adopted the home visiting program in different years for supply- and accreditation-driven reasons, so comparing infant survival and cause-specific mortality in early- versus later-adopting districts, net of district and year fixed effects, identifies the program's effect.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of the home visiting program's arrival in medical subdistricts, 1937-1949, dated by the first year with a non-zero number of visiting nurses in the Medical Report for the Kingdom of Denmark.

units.summary: Danish towns implemented the 1937 home visiting act at different dates because of nurse shortages and accreditation delays, and infant survival is compared before and after each town's start date relative to not-yet-treated towns.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of municipal implementation of the 1937 Danish Act on the Home Visiting Program across Danish towns, 1937-1949; the roll-out was shaped by a shortage and slow inflow of qualified nurses, the DNBH's lengthy accreditation process for nurses and municipal programs, and local preferences of key actors such as GPs and politicians.

units.summary: Event-time dummies around each town's program initiation year trace the dynamics of infant survival, with flat pre-event coefficients supporting the absence of diverging pre-trends.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of municipal implementation of the 1937 home visiting program across Danish towns, 1937-1949, with event-time dummies for the years around each town's initiation year.

units.summary: The same staggered town-level roll-out comparison is re-estimated conditioning on time-varying town socio-economic characteristics, so the effect comes from adoption timing net of observed local conditions.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of municipal implementation of the 1937 home visiting program across Danish towns, 1937-1949, now conditioning on time-varying town socio-economic characteristics.

units.summary: Instead of a binary indicator, program intensity measured as visiting nurses per 1000 live births varies across subdistricts and years, giving a dose-response estimate of the program on infant survival net of subdistrict and year fixed effects.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in the intensity of the program across medical subdistricts and years, measured as nurses per 1000 live births.

units.summary: Quits are regressed on self-reported physical, thermal and chemical hazard exposure in a single survey wave of workers, with identification resting on the claim that, conditional on demographic, job, wage, occupation, industry, region and firm-size controls, hazard exposure is unrelated to the error term.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across workers in self-reported workplace conditions and high involvement work practices in the 2000 DWECS wave; no reform, instrument or discontinuity is used.

atlas.to_label: Propensity to leave the current employer

units.summary: Among workers exposed to the same adverse condition at baseline, those who quit voluntarily are compared with stayers on whether the condition is gone five years later, assuming quitting is as good as random once job-change, education, wage-growth and age controls are included.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in whether the worker separated voluntarily from her firm during 2000, among workers who faced the same adverse condition at baseline; no reform, instrument or discontinuity is used.
